claim: The study recruited 192 participants after excluding 56 who did not meet performance criteria.
source: We recruited a large online sample of participants (N = 192, excluding 56 who did not meet performance criteria; excluded participants did not differ significantly on any psychopathology measure from the retained sample; see Methods)
evidence: The manuscript directly states the sample size and exclusion criteria.

claim: Excluded participants did not differ significantly on any psychopathology measure from the retained sample.
source: We recruited a large online sample of participants (N = 192, excluding 56 who did not meet performance criteria; excluded participants did not differ significantly on any psychopathology measure from the retained sample; see Methods)
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this comparison result.

claim: Participants were less flexible in avoiding punishment than in pursuing reward.
source: In general, participants (n = 192) were less flexible in avoiding punishment than in pursuing reward.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: When instructed to pursue reward, participants often persisted in avoiding features that had previously been associated with punishment, even though at decision time these features were unambiguously benign.
source: Thus, when instructed to pursue reward, participants often persisted in avoiding features that had previously been associated with punishment, even though at decision time these features were unambiguously benign.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Participants showed no significant downregulation of avoidance when punishment avoidance goals were less abundant in the task.
source: In a similar vein, participants showed no significant downregulation of avoidance when punishment avoidance goals were less abundant in the task.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Individuals with chronic worry may have difficulty disengaging from punishment avoidance when instructed to seek reward.
source: Importantly, we show preliminary evidence that individuals with chronic worry may have difficulty disengaging from punishment avoidance when instructed to seek reward.
evidence: This is described as preliminary evidence in the abstract and supported by exploratory analyses.

claim: People avoid punishment less flexibly than they pursue reward.
source: Taken together, the findings demonstrate that people avoid punishment less flexibly than they pursue reward.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: People might devote more resources to pursuing goals involving potential punishment than to goals involving potential reward because of a tendency for losses to loom larger in magnitude than objectively equivalent gains.
source: Thus, people might devote more resources to pursuing goals involving potential punishment than to goals involving potential reward because of a tendency for losses to loom larger in magnitude than objectively equivalent gains (Novemsky and Kahneman, 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on cited literature about loss aversion.

claim: Individuals with pathological anxiety tend to learn more quickly from punishment than reward.
source: Such individuals tend to learn more quickly from punishment than reward (Aylward et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Anxiety is associated with failing to terminate planning in relation to potential threats.
source: Furthermore, evidence suggests that anxiety is associated with failing to terminate planning in relation to potential threats (Berenbaum et al., 2018; Hunter et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The task consisted of 160 trials divided into two equal length blocks.
source: A totality of 160 trials were divided into two equal length blocks, constituting reward- and punishment-rich contexts.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In a reward-rich context, reward seeking trials outnumbered punishment avoidance trials.
source: In a reward-rich context, reward seeking trials outnumbered punishment avoidance trials, and the converse was true in a punishment-rich context.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A model-based strategy was employed to learn the probabilities by which actions led to features for the purpose of flexibly pursuing instructed goals.
source: Whereas a model-based (MB) strategy was employed to learn the probabilities by which actions led to features for the purpose of flexibly pursuing instructed goals
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational modeling analysis.

claim: There was evidence for a model-free strategy that disregarded instructed goals and relied on points won or lost to reinforce actions.
source: there was also evidence for a model-free strategy that disregarded instructed goals and relied on points won or lost to reinforce actions (Lai and Gershman, 2021).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational modeling analysis, with a citation to related work.

claim: Participants used a 'goal perseveration' strategy whereby they learn feature probabilities akin to a model-based strategy but utilize this knowledge in a less costly and less flexible way.
source: Most interestingly, we find evidence for use of a novel strategy we term, 'goal perseveration' (GP), whereby participants learn feature probabilities akin to an MB strategy but utilize this knowledge in a less costly and less flexible way, so as to always avoid punishment (even when instructed to seek reward) and to always seek reward (even when instructed to avoid punishment).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational modeling analysis.

claim: The goal perseveration strategy was used to a greater extent for punishment avoidance.
source: Strikingly, this GP strategy was used to a greater extent for punishment avoidance, suggesting that disengaging punishment avoidance is harder, perhaps for evolutionarily sensible reasons (Woody and Szechtman, 2011).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational modeling analysis, with speculation about evolutionary reasons.

claim: The more flexible model-based strategy was leveraged to a greater degree during reward seeking.
source: By contrast, the more flexible MB strategy was leveraged to a greater degree during reward seeking.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational modeling analysis.

claim: Participants flexibly increased model-based control toward reward seeking goals when they were more abundant.
source: Furthermore, participants flexibly increased MB control toward reward seeking goals when they were more abundant.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational modeling analysis.

claim: The degree of reliance on a goal perseveration strategy to avoid punishment was positively associated with dispositional worry.
source: In so doing, we found preliminary evidence that the degree of reliance on a GP strategy to avoid punishment was positively associated with dispositional worry, which appears to be unique to those expressing worry and not to individuals with obsessive–compulsive (OC) or somatic anxiety symptoms.
evidence: This is described as preliminary evidence from exploratory analyses.

claim: A unique signature of model-based control in the task manifests in goal-switch trials in the way the current goal determines whether observed features in the last trial impact subsequent action.
source: By simulating an artificial MB agent, we show that a unique signature of MB control in our task manifests, when current and previous goals differ (henceforth referred to as 'goal-switch' trials), in the way the current goal determines whether observed features in the last trial impact subsequent action.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation of an artificial agent.

claim: A model-based agent will avoid an action leading to a punishment feature in the last trial only when the current instructed goal is to avoid punishment.
source: For example, an MB agent will avoid an action leading to a punishment feature in the last trial only when the current instructed goal is to avoid punishment (Figure 2A, top row).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A unique signature of a model-free strategy is how a previous goal determines the impact of last observed features on subsequent action, regardless of whether the goal has switched.
source: Since the previous goal is what determines the value of the last observed features, a unique signature of an MF strategy is how a previous goal determines the impact of last observed features on subsequent action, regardless of whether the goal has switched.
evidence: This is explained through logical inference about the model-free strategy.

claim: If an action led to a punishment on the last trial, a model-free agent will tend to avoid that action irrespective of the current goal.
source: For example, if an action led to a punishment on the last trial, then that action will tend to be avoided irrespective of the current goal (Figure 2A, bottom row).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A goal perseveration agent will avoid an action that led to a punishment feature at the last trial even if both previous and current goals were to seek reward.
source: For example, a GP agent will avoid an action that led to a punishment feature at the last trial even if both previous and current goals were to seek reward (Figure 2A, middle row).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A model-based strategy in the task led to significantly more reward than the other strategies.
source: This showed that an MB strategy in our task led to significantly more reward than the other strategies (Figure 3A; e.g., around 40% more than a GP agent), and only 15% worse than an idealized model that has access to the true feature probabilities for each action.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The advantage of the model-based strategy was due in large part to the task involving frequent goal switching (41.8% of trials).
source: The advantage of the MB strategy was due in large part to the task involving frequent goal switching (41.8% of trials).
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: The least costly model-free strategy also earns the least reward in the present task.
source: Finally, the least costly MF strategy also earns the least reward in the present task (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Participants leveraged model-based control for both reward seeking and punishment avoidance goals.
source: Posterior estimates showed that individuals engaged MB control for both reward seeking (mode = −0.52, CI = [−0.69,−0.38], pd = 1) and punishment avoidance goals was highly trending (mode = 0.12, CI = [−0.01,0.28], pd = 0.96).
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian regression analysis.

claim: There was a larger model-based effect for reward seeking than for punishment avoidance.
source: Moreover, we found a larger MB effect for reward seeking than for punishment avoidance (mode = 0.41, CI = [0.20,0.62], pd = 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian regression analysis.

claim: A model-free strategy was employed by participants both in response to reward and punishment.
source: Posterior estimates showed a MF strategy was employed by participants (MF main effect mode = 0.24, CI = 0.14,0.36, pd = 1), both in response to reward (mode = −0.14, CI = [−0.23,−0.04]; Figure 2C, bottom row) and punishment (mode = 0.22, CI = [0.12,0.31]).
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian regression analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There was no evidence that the valence of the feedback impacted model-free behavior to a greater degree.
source: We found no evidence that the valence of the feedback impacted MF behavior to a greater degree (mode = −0.08, CI = [−0.21,0.06], pd = 0.87).
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian regression analysis.

claim: Goal perseveration was utilized for punishment avoidance significantly more so than for reward seeking.
source: Breaking the GP effect down by valence showed that GP was utilized for punishment avoidance (mode = 0.33, CI = [0.20,0.45], pd = 1), significantly more so than for reward seeking (mode = −0.11, CI = [−0.23,0.02], pd = 0.95; difference between goals: mode = −0.20, CI = [−0.37,−0.04], pd = 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian regression analysis.

claim: Allowing the model to adjust model-based utilization based on goal abundance improved model fit significantly.
source: Allowing the model to adjust in this way improved an index of model fit significantly (Δ iBIC = −175.95; Figure 4A) providing evidence that individuals reallocated MB resources toward goals that were more abundant.
evidence: This is a finding from the model comparison analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The MBRR + MF model's fit was superior to the MBRR model.
source: The MBRR+ MF models' fit was superior to the MBRR model (Δ iBIC = −896.72; Figure 4A), providing evidence that individuals used both MF and MBRR strategies to inform their decisions.
evidence: This is a finding from the model comparison analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Enhancing the MBRR + MF model with the addition of a goal perseveration strategy significantly improved model fit.
source: Enhancing the MBRR + MF with the addition of a GP strategy significantly improved model fit (Δ iBIC = −243.73; Figure 4A), indicating participants also used a GP strategy.
evidence: This is a finding from the model comparison analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Individuals relied significantly more on a model-based strategy for reward seeking relative to punishment avoidance.
source: In doing so, we found that individuals relied significantly more on an MB strategy for reward seeking relative to punishment avoidance (two-tailed p < 0.001, nonparametric test [see Methods]; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from the parameter analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Individuals relied more heavily on goal perseveration for punishment avoidance relative to reward seeking.
source: By contrast, individuals relied more heavily on GP for punishment avoidance relative to reward seeking (two-tailed p = 0.026, nonparametric test; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the parameter analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Individuals were sensitive to reward goal abundance.
source: This analysis revealed that individuals were sensitive to reward goal abundance (mean = 0.50, p = <0.001)
evidence: This is a finding from the parameter analysis.

claim: Individuals were not sensitive to punishment goal abundance.
source: but not to punishment goal abundance (mean = −0.13, p = 0.13).
evidence: This is a finding from the parameter analysis.

claim: There was no significant or trending relationship between any form of psychopathology and model-based control for punishment avoidance.
source: However, we found no significant or trending relationships between any form of psychopathology and MB control for punishment avoidance (Figure 5A, left column).
evidence: This is a finding from the exploratory analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There was initial evidence of a potential relationship between the tendency to worry and punishment avoidance perseveration.
source: In so doing we found initial evidence of a potential relationship between the tendency to worry and punishment avoidance perseveration (B = 2.15, t = 1.4, p = 0.16; Figure 5A, right column).
evidence: This is described as initial evidence from the exploratory analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: When controlling for covariates, there was a stronger relationship between worry and punishment perseveration.
source: This analysis showed a stronger relationship between worry and punishment perseveration (β = 3.14 (1.38), t = 2.27, p = 0.04, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the exploratory analysis with covariates shown in Figure 5B.

claim: No other significant relationship was observed between punishment perseveration or model-based punishment avoidance and psychopathology.
source: No other significant relationship was observed between punishment perseveration or MB punishment avoidance and psychopathology (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from the exploratory analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A goal perseveration + model-based agent that adaptively engages reward-relevant information when instructed to, but perseverates in avoiding punishment during reward seeking, is as good as a model-based agent in avoiding punishment.
source: We show that such a strategy is as good as an MB agent in avoiding punishment, but comes with the cost of suboptimal reward seeking (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: A goal perseveration + model-based agent comes with the cost of suboptimal reward seeking.
source: We show that such a strategy is as good as an MB agent in avoiding punishment, but comes with the cost of suboptimal reward seeking (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: The strategic deployment of goal perseveration primarily toward punishment avoidance indicates such behavior is not merely a reflection of a noisy or forgetful model-based system.
source: The strategic deployment of GP primarily toward punishment avoidance indicates such behavior is not merely a reflection of a noisy or forgetful MB system.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental findings.

claim: The finding that humans use less flexible computational strategies to avoid punishment than to seek reward aligns with the idea of distinct neural mechanisms supporting avoidance and approach behavior.
source: Our finding that humans use less flexible computational strategies to avoid punishment, than to seek reward, aligns with the idea of distinct neural mechanisms supporting avoidance and approach behavior (McNaughton and Gray, 2000; Lang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the findings to cited literature.

claim: Comparative ethology and evolutionary psychology suggest there are good reasons why punishment avoidance might be less flexible than reward seeking.
source: Moreover, comparative ethology and evolutionary psychology (Pinker, 1997) suggest there are good reasons why punishment avoidance might be less flexible than reward seeking.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited literature.

claim: To reduce the potentially deadly occurrence of false negative errors (failure to prepare for upcoming danger), it is adaptive for the system to tolerate a high rate of false positive errors (false alarms).
source: Woody and Szechtman, 2011 opined that 'to reduce the potentially deadly occurrence of false negative errors (failure to prepare for upcoming danger), it is adaptive for the system to tolerate a high rate of false positive errors (false alarms).'
evidence: This is a quote from cited literature.

claim: In the presence of multiple shifting goals, perseverance in punishment avoidance results in false positives during reward seeking.
source: Indeed, we demonstrate that in the presence of multiple shifting goals, perseverance in punishment avoidance results in false positives during reward seeking (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Perseverance in punishment avoidance avoids 'missing' punishment avoidance opportunities because of lapses in goal switching.
source: but avoids 'missing' punishment avoidance opportunities because of lapses in goal switching (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Goal perseveration may constitute a resource rational strategy for approximating model-based control.
source: GP may thus in fact constitute an RR strategy (Lieder and Griffiths, 2019) for approximating MB control.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation with a citation to the resource rationality framework.

claim: Model-based learning is computationally demanding in the task specifically because goals switch between trials.
source: To illustrate this, consider that MB learning is computationally demanding in our task specifically because goals switch between trials.
evidence: This is an inference about the computational demands of the task.

claim: Goal perseveration avoids computationally costly operations by pursuing goals persistently, thus avoiding switching and ensuring that features are equally relevant for planning and learning.
source: GP avoids these computationally costly operations by pursuing goals persistently, thus avoiding switching and ensuring that features are equally relevant for planning and learning.
evidence: This is an inference about how goal perseveration reduces computational costs.

claim: Goal perseveration saves substantial computational resources compared to model-based control yet is able to perform relatively well on the task, achieving better performance than model-free.
source: In this way, GP saves substantial computational resources compared to MB yet is able to perform relatively well on the task, achieving better performance than MF.
evidence: This is an inference about the computational efficiency and performance of goal perseveration.

claim: If a participant selectively cares about avoiding losses (for instance, due to loss aversion), goal perseveration can perform as well as model-based control.
source: Additionally, if a participant selectively cares about avoiding losses (for instance, due to loss aversion), GP can perform as well as MB.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference about when goal perseveration might be optimal.

claim: The goal perseveration heuristic reflects a strategic choice, which can achieve good performance while avoiding the substantial resource requirements associated with model-based control.
source: Thus, we propose the GP heuristic reflects a strategic choice, which can achieve good performance while avoiding the substantial resource requirements associated with MB control.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the findings.

claim: The exploratory findings that an inflexibility in punishment avoidance was more pronounced in individuals with chronic worry is suggestive of a computational deficit that may serve to unify several known effects relating trait worry to failure to terminate threat processing.
source: Our exploratory findings that an inflexibility in punishment avoidance was more pronounced in individuals with chronic worry is suggestive of a computational deficit that may serve to unify several known effects relating trait worry to failure to terminate threat processing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the exploratory findings.

claim: In paradigms that explicitly instruct participants to ignore threat-irrelevant information, individuals with trait worry have difficulty inhibiting processing of threat.
source: For example, in paradigms that explicitly instruct participants to ignore threat-irrelevant information, such as the dot-probe (Asmundson and Stein, 1994) and modified emotional Stroop (Dalgleish, 1995; van den Hout et al., 1995) tasks, individuals with trait worry have difficulty inhibiting processing of threat (Bar-Haim et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Increased goal perseveration punishment avoidance may be involved in the overactivity of threat-related circuitry in anxious individuals during tasks where threat is not present.
source: Moreover, increased GP punishment avoidance may be involved in the overactivity of threat-related circuitry in anxious individuals during tasks where threat is not present (Grupe and Nitschke, 2013; Nitschke et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with citations to prior research.

claim: The findings go beyond previous findings that report, in single-goal reinforcement learning tasks, that anxiety is associated with altered model-free but intact model-based control.
source: Our findings go beyond previous findings that report, in single-goal reinforcement learning tasks, that anxiety is associated with altered MF but intact MB control (Gillan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior research with a citation.

claim: A conflict between punishment avoidance and reward seeking may be necessary to uncover how knowledge of task structure is used in anxiety.
source: Our findings suggest a conflict between punishment avoidance and reward seeking may be necessary to uncover how knowledge of task structure is used in anxiety.
evidence: This is an inference from the findings.

claim: Prior approach–avoidance conflict paradigms have found that trait anxiety is positively associated with neural correlates of punishment avoidance (rejected gambles that could result in loss).
source: Indeed, prior approach–avoidance conflict paradigms have found that trait anxiety is positively associated with neural correlates of punishment avoidance (rejected gambles that could result in loss) (Loh et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Prior approach–avoidance conflict paradigms have found that trait anxiety is positively associated with avoidant behavior.
source: and avoidant behavior (Bach, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Differences in strategy utilization for reward seeking and punishment avoidance could in part reflect differences in sensitivity to reward versus punishment.
source: A limitation of our task is that differences in strategy utilization for reward seeking and punishment avoidance (see Methods) could in part reflect differences in sensitivity to reward versus punishment.
evidence: This is acknowledged as a limitation.

claim: Reward and punishment sensitivity cannot account for the effects observed across strategies, since punishment avoidance was greater for goal perseveration, whereas reward seeking was greater within a model-based framework.
source: However, reward and punishment sensitivity cannot account for the effects we observe across strategies, since on the one hand, punishment avoidance was greater for GP, whereas reward seeking was greater within an MB framework.
evidence: This is an inference from the pattern of results.

claim: Knowledge of reward features had a greater net impact on choice across both goal-oriented strategies (sum of weights across both model-based and goal perseveration strategies is greater for reward seeking).
source: Moreover, knowledge of reward features had a greater net impact on choice across both goal-oriented strategies (sum of weights across both MB and GP strategies is greater for reward seeking).
evidence: This is an inference from the parameter estimates.

claim: Differences in outcome sensitivity, which are algorithmically equivalent to differences in the magnitude of external incentives, may cause a shift from one strategy to another.
source: That said, we recognize that differences in outcome sensitivity, which are algorithmically equivalent to differences in the magnitude of external incentives, may cause a shift from one strategy to another (Kool et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculation with a citation to prior research.

claim: Termination failures in chronic worry are dissociable from a tendency to suffer 'initiation' failures, which involve worrying too easily in response to many stimuli.
source: The causal role of GP in failures to terminate worry episodes could avail of the fact that such failures are dissociable from a tendency to suffer 'initiation' failures, which involve worrying too easily in response to many stimuli (Berenbaum et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Punishment avoidance in obsessive-compulsive symptoms has been empirically demonstrated to be specific to idiographic domains of potential threat (e.g., sanitation).
source: Although the perseveration of worry may appear relevant to obsessions in OC symptoms, punishment avoidance in OC has been empirically demonstrated to be specific to idiographic domains of potential threat (e.g., sanitation Amir et al., 2009), an issue the present study did not investigate.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The study did not find that goal perseveration was associated with somatic anxiety possibly due perhaps to random sampling error as there was an unusually low percentage meeting a threshold for mild symptomatology (4.7%).
source: Additionally, we did not find that GP was associated with somatic anxiety possibly due perhaps to random sampling error as we had an unusually low percentage meeting a threshold for mild symptomatology (4.7%; typical convenience samples are typically in the range of 12–18 Sharp et al., 2015; Telch et al., 1989).
evidence: This is an interpretation of a null finding with citations to prior research.

claim: Somatic anxiety is thought to involve lower-order cognitive processes than those likely involved in multigoal pursuit.
source: More importantly, somatic anxiety is thought to involve lower-order cognitive processes than those likely involved in multigoal pursuit (Sharp et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Two hundred and forty-eight participants were recruited through Prolific services online recruiting service from English-speaking countries.
source: Two hundred and forty-eight participants were recruited through Prolific services online Prolific recruiting service (https://www.prolific.co/) using the final task design from English-speaking countries to ensure participants understood task instruction.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.

claim: After expected data-scrubbing, the sample size had >99% power to detect valence differences in reinforcement learning parameters, conservatively assuming a medium effect size relative to large effects found previously.
source: After expected data-scrubbing, our sample size had >99% power to detect valence differences in reinforcement learning parameters, conservatively assuming a medium effect size relative to large effects found previously (to account for differences between multigoal and single-goal settings; e.g., Palminteri et al., 2017; Lefebvre et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a power analysis with citations to prior research.

claim: The sample had >80% power to detect small-medium effect sizes relating computational parameters and individual differences in anxiety.
source: Moreover, our sample had >80% power to detect small-medium effect sizes relating computational parameters and individual differences in anxiety ( Sharp et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a power analysis with a citation to prior research.

claim: The final sample was 37% male, with a mean age of 33.92 years (standard deviation = 11.97).
source: The final sample was 37% male, with a mean age of 33.92 years (standard deviation [SD] = 11.97).
evidence: This is demographic data stated in the Methods section.

claim: Rates of mild but clinically relevant levels of OCD (45%) and worry (40%) comported with prior studies, indicating good representation of individual variation in at least some psychopathological symptoms.
source: Rates of mild but clinically relevant levels of OCD (45%) and worry (40%) comported with prior studies (Sharp et al., 2021), indicating good representation of individual variation in at least some psychopathological symptoms.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior research with a citation.

claim: Eleven participants completed less than 90% of the trials and were removed.
source: Eleven participants completed less than 90% of the trials and were removed.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.

claim: Six participants were removed because their switch behavior was the exact opposite as they should be for each of the four learning signals.
source: We removed six additional participants because their switch behavior was the exact opposite as they should be for each of these four learning signals.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.

claim: Thirteen participants were removed for treating a punishment feature as a reward feature.
source: We additionally removed participants that: (1) treating a punishment feature as a reward feature (i.e., show the opposite of the two learning signals for punishment; 13 participants)
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.

claim: Twenty-six participants were removed for treating reward feature as a punishment feature.
source: and (2) treating reward feature as a punishment feature (show the opposite of the two learning signals for reward; 26 participants).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.

claim: Excluded subjects performed significantly worse in terms of choice accuracy.
source: Excluded subjects performed significantly worse in terms of choice accuracy.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.

claim: On average, excluded subjects chose correctly 49.6% of time, whereas included subjects chose correctly 63.5% of time.
source: On average, excluded subjects chose correctly 49.6% of time, whereas included subjects chose correctly 63.5% of time (difference between groups: t(190) = 9.66, p < 0.00001).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.

claim: Removed participants were no different in terms of mean scores on key measures of psychopathology.
source: Importantly, removed participants were no different in terms of mean scores on key measures of psychopathology (greatest mean difference found in OCD; Welch's t = −0.96, p = 0.33).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.

claim: Chronic worry was measured via the 16-item Penn State Worry Questionnaire.
source: Chronic worry was measured via the 16-item Penn State Worry Questionnaire (Meyer et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section with a citation.

claim: Anxious arousal was measured with the 10-question mini version of the Mood and Anxiety Symptom Questionnaire – Anxious Arousal subscale.
source: Anxious arousal was measured with the 10-question mini version of the Mood and Anxiety Symptom Questionnaire – Anxious Arousal subscale (Casillas and Clark, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section with a citation.

claim: Obsessive compulsiveness was measured with the Obsessive Compulsive Inventory – Revised.
source: Obsessive compulsiveness was measured with the Obsessive Compulsive Inventory – Revised (Foa et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section with a citation.

claim: The task consisted of 160 trials.
source: The task consisted of 160 trials.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.

claim: On each trial, participants had 4 s to make a choice between two choice options (represented as fractal images).
source: On each trial, participants had 4 s to make a choice between two choice options (represented as fractal images; (Figure 1B)).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The probabilities linking features to actions varied over time, and participants could estimate these continuously drifting probabilities from experience by observing which features actions led to.
source: The probabilities linking features to actions varied over time, and participants could estimate these continuously drifting probabilities from experience by observing which features actions led to.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.

claim: Presenting both actual and counterfactual outcomes removed the need for participants to explore less-visited actions to gain information, thus ruling out information seeking as a normative explanation for deviations from optimal choice.
source: Presenting both actual and counterfactual outcomes removed the need for participants to explore less-visited actions to gain information, thus ruling out information seeking as a normative explanation for deviations from optimal choice.
evidence: This is an inference about the task design.

claim: This task design differs from influential two-factor learning paradigms extensively used to study anxiety, in that in the task both action-feature and feature-value associations changed throughout the experiment, mandating continued learning and flexible decision-making.
source: Of note, this task design differs from influential two-factor learning paradigms (Mowrer, 1951) extensively used to study anxiety, in that in our task both action-feature and feature-value associations changed throughout the experiment, mandating continued learning and flexible decision-making.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior paradigms with a citation.

claim: Models were fit with a hierarchical variant of expectation–maximization algorithm known as iterative importance sampling.
source: Models were fit with a hierarchical variant of expectation–maximization algorithm known as iterative importance sampling (Bishop, 2006), which has been shown to provide high parameter and model recoverability (Michely et al., 2020b; Michely et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section with citations.

claim: Key inverse temperature parameters were successfully recovered (all above 0.58 correlation, average correlation = 0.79).
source: To verify that the experiment was appropriately designed to dissociate between the tested models and their parameter values, we simulated experimental data from the best-fitting and reduced models and successfully recovered key inverse temperature parameters (all above 0.58 correlation, average correlation = 0.79).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.

claim: The model that generated the data was recovered 10/10 times compared to the next best-fitting model.
source: The model that generated the data was recovered 10/10 times compared to the next best-fitting model (see Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.
